summary: Defines the application/vnd.pwg-multiplexed content type for objects made of several parts. Like multipart/related, it holds a sequence of chunks, each containing a MIME message or part of one, that together make up the whole object.

eli5.summary: Some things come in many pieces, like a set of parts. This label describes one package that carries several smaller messages in a line.

questions: how to package multiple mime messages in one object
when should i use multiplexed instead of multipart
how do chunks work in the pwg format
what are the use cases for pwg-multiplexed
subtitle: A MIME type for packaging multi-component documents with interleaved parts

tldr.problem: Compound documents (like a web page with embedded images) need to be packaged for transmission. The standard multipart/related format requires all images to come either before or after the document, causing delays and storage problems.
tldr.mechanism: Application/Vnd.pwg-multiplexed chunks messages into pieces of specified length, allowing images and other components to be interleaved with the document that references them, arriving close to where they are needed.
tldr.outcome: Printers and scanners can process documents and images efficiently without waiting for all parts to arrive or buffering large amounts of data, improving performance in resource-constrained environments.

today: RFC 3391 is an Informational standard defining a vendor-specific MIME type. While it has not seen universal adoption for general web use, it is employed in print-related technologies and embedded document systems (such as the MHTML format for saved web pages) where streaming efficiency and just-in-time delivery of components matter. The format demonstrates an alternative approach to Multipart/Related for scenarios where component interleaving is beneficial.

sections.title: Packaging Compound Documents
sections.content:
A compound object consists of multiple related components: a text document with embedded images, for example. Each component needs to be transmitted or stored, and there must be a way to identify how the components relate to each other.

The existing Multipart/Related MIME type allows this, but with a limitation: all component parts are presented as a sequence. If a document references images, those images must either all come before the document (requiring the producer to know all images upfront and the consumer to buffer them) or all come after (requiring the consumer to wait and read the entire document before printing).

The RFC defines Application/Vnd.pwg-multiplexed as an alternative. Instead of body parts separated by boundary markers, it uses chunks of specified length, allowing components to be interleaved. A chunk can contain part of one message, and the next chunk can contain part of a different message. This allows images to be positioned immediately before or after the place where they are referenced.
sections.eli5: Instead of "here are all the pictures, then here is the document," or "here is the document, then all the pictures," you can say "here is part of the document, here is a picture it mentions, here is more of the document."

sections.title: Understanding Chunks and Messages
sections.content:
The format introduces specific terminology:

A message is a single component of the compound object, such as a complete document or a complete image. It has MIME headers and content, just like a body part in Multipart/Related.

A chunk is a piece of data with a header specifying its message number and length. A message can be split across multiple chunks. The chunks for a given message number must be in order, but chunks from different messages can be interleaved.

Each chunk header contains: the keyword CHK, a message number, the length of the payload in octets, and a marker indicating whether this is the last chunk of that message (LAST) or more chunks will follow (MORE). The format ends with a final chunk having message number 0, length 0, and LAST.

The first chunk must contain the root message—the primary document that references other components. Additional chunks contain the referenced components.
sections.eli5: Each piece has a label saying which message it belongs to and how many bytes are in it. When the message is done, it gets marked as LAST. When everything is finished, you send a special CHK 0 0 LAST marker.

sections.title: Technical Structure
sections.content:
The MIME Content-Type header for an Application/Vnd.pwg-multiplexed entity specifies a required type parameter, which is the content-type of the root message. This allows receivers to know what they are looking at without reading the entire stream.

The body is a sequence of chunks. Each chunk consists of:

  • A chunk header: CHK 1 550 LAST (for example)
  • The payload: the octets of the message
  • A CRLF (carriage return, line feed) for visual separation

The syntax is deliberately simple: no boundary markers to scan for, just a header specifying the exact byte count. This eliminates ambiguity—the receiver knows exactly how many bytes to read.

A single message can be split across multiple chunks, with chunks potentially separated by chunks from other messages. The order of chunks within a message must be preserved. Chunk payloads can be zero bytes long (for example, to satisfy a requirement that the root message starts at the first chunk without any leading bytes), allowing programming flexibility.

Each message is intended to be byte-for-byte identical to a corresponding body part in an equivalent Multipart/Related entity. Messages can include MIME headers like Content-Type, Content-ID, and Content-Location to identify and reference components.
sections.eli5: The format is strict: a header that says "next chunk is 500 bytes," then exactly 500 bytes, then a line break. No ambiguity, no scanning for markers.

sections.title: Processing and Use Cases
sections.content:
A receiver that recognizes Application/Vnd.pwg-multiplexed and understands the content-type of the root message can display the compound object as intended, assembling chunks in message number order.

The RFC motivates this format with printing, scanning, and web-to-print workflows where timing matters:

High-speed printing: A printer receives page descriptions (the root component) that reference images. With Multipart/Related, the printer must either wait for all images upfront (delaying printing) or read the entire document before starting (requiring large buffers). With multiplexed chunks, each image arrives just before its first reference, so the printer can start printing immediately.

Scanning to print: A scanner produces pages and sends them with a document containing references to each page. Images cannot come before the root component if the printer lacks buffer space. Images cannot come after if the printer has already started and moved on. Chunking allows images to arrive just-in-time.

The RFC emphasizes that receivers must guard against malicious producers that send many interleaved messages or references to non-existent components, potentially exhausting storage. Well-designed receivers set limits on the number of concurrent messages and the amount of data they buffer.
sections.eli5: A printer can be printing one part while receiving the next part, so it doesn't have to wait or buffer everything. But the receiver has to be careful that a malicious sender doesn't try to make it buffer infinite data.

sections.title: Examples and Strategies
sections.content:
The RFC provides multiple examples of the same compound object (an XHTML document with three images) represented in different ways:

One example puts each complete message into its own chunk, equivalent to Multipart/Related.

Another example splits the XHTML root message into three chunks interleaved with image chunks, positioning images to appear shortly before the text that references them.

A third example splits the XHTML into four chunks and splits images into two chunks each, showing how fine-grained chunking can be.

The final example demonstrates that empty chunks are allowed—a message can end with an empty LAST chunk, or the root message can start with an empty chunk (causing the real root message to begin in the second chunk). This flexibility eases implementation: a producer can avoid careful bookkeeping by chunking whenever its buffer fills, even if that creates adjacent chunks with the same message number.

The RFC emphasizes that strategies for arranging chunks depend on the document structure. Vertically stacked blocks (text, then image, then more text) map naturally to sequential chunks. Side-by-side images require the producer and consumer to negotiate buffering. Run-around text (text wrapping beside an image) requires the producer to guess where the image should end and the next block should begin, with fallback display strategies if the guess is wrong.
sections.eli5: You can arrange chunks in many ways depending on your document. The examples show that simple documents chunk easily, and complex layouts need care but are still possible.
